title: Sunset & Sunrise IOL Syndromes: Navigating Post-Operative Decentration
summary: Sunset and Sunrise syndromes represent distinct patterns of Intraocular Lens (IOL) decentration resulting from zonular instability, asymmetric haptic placement, or capsular bag contraction. This guide details the clinical recognition and surgical management of these malpositioned lenses.

branches: Sunset Syndrome: Inferior decentration of the IOL where the superior edge of the optic is visible in the pupillary axis.
Sunrise Syndrome: Superior decentration of the IOL where the inferior edge of the optic is visible in the pupillary axis.
Windshield Wiper: Lateral oscillating movement of a sulcus-placed IOL due to inadequate haptic-to-haptic diameter.
Lost Lens: Complete dislocation into the vitreous cavity.

sections.title: Sunset vs. Sunrise: The Comparative Anatomy

rows: Superior zonular dialysis or gravity (one haptic in bag, one in sulcus)
Asymmetric haptic placement (superior haptic in sulcus, inferior haptic in bag) + fibrosis

sections.title: Etiology & Risk Factors
content: Zonular Laxity: PXF, Marfan syndrome, Homocystinuria, Weill-Marchesani.
Trauma: Blunt ocular trauma causing zonular dialysis.
Surgical Factors: Asymmetrical haptic placement (one haptic out/one in).
Capsular Factors: Progressive capsular phimosis and bag contraction.
High Myopia: Longer axial lengths (≥26.5mm) correlate with larger capsular bags and weaker zonules.
Previous Vitrectomy: Reduced vitreous support for the lens capsule.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Sudden decrease in visual acuity with new monocular diplopia.
Uveitis-Glaucoma-Hyphema (UGH) Syndrome: Haptic rubbing against the posterior iris.
Vitreous in the anterior chamber (sign of zonular/capsular rupture).
Retinal detachment associated with posterior IOL migration.
Phacodonesis or IOL-donesis on slit-lamp examination.

sections.title: The Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Dilated Slit Lamp Exam: Assess IOL centration, haptic position, and zonular integrity.
2. Retroillumination Photography: Essential to document the optic-pupil relationship.
3. Gonioscopy: Check for haptic erosion or iris tucking.
4. Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM): The gold standard for identifying haptic location (In-the-bag vs. Sulcus).
5. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Assess for Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) secondary to inflammation.

rows: Induces high astigmatism but optic center remains in axis
Occurs in phakic patients; phacodonesis present
Vision loss without diplopia or edge glare
Obscured red reflex; different clinical history

sections.title: Grading of Decentration (AAO/Guyton)
content: Grade 1: <1mm decentration (Usually asymptomatic).
Grade 2: 1-2mm decentration (Edge of optic visible in pupil).
Grade 3: 2-3mm decentration (Visual axis near edge of optic).
Grade 4: >3mm decentration (Visual axis outside of the optic).

sections.title: Surgical Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Observation if asymptomatic and stable.
Step 2: Miotics (Pilocarpine) for mild cases with edge-glare.
Step 3: Surgical Repositioning (McCannel or Siepser Suture).
Step 4: Scleral Fixation (Yamane Technique or Gore-Tex Suture).
Step 5: IOL Exchange (AC-IOL or Scleral-Fixated PCIOL).

rows: Mild to moderate decentration with intact iris
Total lack of capsular support; 3-piece IOL
Scleral suture fixation without conjunctival peritomy
Scleral-fixated PCIOL with Gore-Tex or Prolene

content.explanation: S: Superior haptic in Sulcus; U: Under-bag inferior haptic; N: Noted Sunrise; U: Upward shift; P: Phimosis/Fibrosis often contributes.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & High-Yield Facts
content: 1-Piece Acrylic IOLs should NEVER be placed in the sulcus (high risk of UGH).
3-Piece IOLs are the 'workhorse' for repositioning due to thin, flexible PMMA haptics.
If the IOL is sunsetting, check the superior zonules first.
YAG capsulotomy can sometimes worsen decentration if the bag is already unstable.
Wait at least 3-6 months post-op before deciding on surgery if the vision is functional.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Retinal Detachment: Higher risk during IOL manipulation/exchange.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Common after secondary IOL procedures.
Corneal Decompensation: Risk of endothelial cell loss during AC-IOL insertion.
Secondary Glaucoma: Pigment dispersion or UGH syndrome.
Endophthalmitis: Rare risk with any intraocular re-entry.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The Yamane Influence
sections.content: The Flanged Intrascleral Haptic Fixation (Yamane Technique) has revolutionized the management of Sunrise/Sunset syndromes. By using 30-gauge needles to create scleral tunnels and cautery to create haptic 'bulbs,' surgeons can securely fixate a 3-piece IOL without sutures. This has significantly reduced the operative time and long-term risk of suture degradation (e.g., 10-0 Prolene snapping).
